title: Parkinson's disease: diagnosis and drug management
subject: neurology
setting: Outpatient, neurology and geriatric clinic, hospital ward
summary: Diagnose clinically (bradykinesia with rest tremor or rigidity), refer untreated to a specialist, offer levodopa when motor symptoms affect quality of life, warn about impulse control disorders and sleepiness with dopamine agonists, never stop dopaminergic drugs abruptly, and give doses on time in hospital.

sections.title: Diagnosis
items: Parkinsonism: bradykinesia plus rest tremor, rigidity or both (MDS 2015 criteria). Supportive features: clear response to levodopa, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, rest tremor of a limb, loss of smell.
Refer suspected Parkinson's disease quickly and untreated to a specialist (NICE). Review the diagnosis every 6 to 12 months and reconsider it if atypical features develop.

Red flags for another cause: early falls, rapid progression, early severe autonomic failure, vertical gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, early dementia, parkinsonism limited to the legs, no response to high-dose levodopa.
Drug-induced parkinsonism: ask about antipsychotics, metoclopramide and prochlorperazine and, commonly in India, levosulpiride, flunarizine and cinnarizine; stop the drug where possible.

Do not use structural MRI to diagnose Parkinson's disease; it helps exclude vascular parkinsonism or normal pressure hydrocephalus. Consider DaTscan (123I-FP-CIT SPECT) if essential tremor cannot be distinguished clinically.

sections.title: Starting treatment (NICE NG71, MDS review)
items: Discuss options: levodopa gives the most improvement in motor symptoms and daily living but more motor complications; dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors give less benefit, and agonists cause more sleepiness, hallucinations and impulse control disorders.
Offer levodopa (with carbidopa or benserazide) in early Parkinson's disease when motor symptoms affect quality of life.

If motor symptoms do not affect quality of life, choose levodopa, a non-ergot dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine) or an MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, selegiline). Do not use ergot-derived agonists first line.

Before starting, warn (and record) about impulse control disorders, excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep onset, and hallucinations. Advise informing the driving licence authority and not driving if sleepy.
Refer for Parkinson's physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy (speech, swallow, saliva); encourage regular exercise and advise vitamin D supplementation.

sections.title: Motor fluctuations and dyskinesia
items: Wearing off or dyskinesia: seek specialist advice before changing treatment. Options added to levodopa: a dopamine agonist, an MAO-B inhibitor or a COMT inhibitor (entacapone, opicapone). Consider amantadine for dyskinesia.
Do not give anticholinergics to people with motor fluctuations or dyskinesia.
A protein redistribution diet (most protein in the evening meal) may help fluctuations; do not reduce total daily protein.
Advanced disease: apomorphine injection or infusion, levodopa intestinal gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa or deep brain stimulation in specialist centres.

sections.title: Hospital admission and nil by mouth
items: Never stop or suddenly reduce levodopa or other dopaminergic drugs (including during gastroenteritis or surgery): risk of acute akinesia, aspiration and a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. No drug holidays.
Give Parkinson's medicines at the patient's own times, ideally within 30 minutes of the due time; allow self-medication where safe and record exact timings on admission.

Nil by mouth or unsafe swallow: give dispersible levodopa via a nasogastric tube, or a rotigotine patch if enteral access is impossible, using a conversion calculator and specialist advice. Resume usual oral drugs as soon as possible.
Avoid dopamine antagonists: haloperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol and typical antipsychotics. For nausea use domperidone (check QTc) or ondansetron (never with apomorphine).

Delirium or agitation: treat the cause first; if a sedative is unavoidable, prefer a low-dose benzodiazepine (lorazepam 0.5 to 1 mg orally, max 2 mg in 24 hours, per the Scottish Delirium Association pathway) and seek specialist advice.

sections.title: Non-motor symptoms and complications
items: Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, shopping) can occur with any dopaminergic drug, most with agonists, and are often concealed: ask at every review. Reduce the agonist gradually first and watch for agonist withdrawal.

Hallucinations or delusions: look for infection, dehydration or new drugs; do not treat if well tolerated; reduce the likely culprit drug with specialist advice; then consider quetiapine, or clozapine with blood monitoring. Do not use olanzapine.
Orthostatic hypotension: review antihypertensives, diuretics, dopaminergic drugs, anticholinergics and antidepressants; then consider midodrine (monitor for supine hypertension) or fludrocortisone.
Parkinson's disease dementia: offer a cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine or donepezil) for mild to moderate dementia; memantine only if these are not tolerated or are contraindicated.
Excessive daytime sleepiness or sudden sleep onset: no driving; adjust medicines with specialist advice. REM sleep behaviour disorder: consider clonazepam or melatonin.
Treat depression, anxiety, constipation, urinary symptoms and pain actively. Drooling: speech and language therapy, then glycopyrronium or botulinum toxin via a specialist.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling drug-induced or vascular parkinsonism, essential tremor or progressive supranuclear palsy as Parkinson's disease.
Missed or delayed levodopa doses during admission, fasting or surgery.
Prescribing metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or haloperidol for nausea, vomiting or delirium.
Stopping a dopamine agonist abruptly: agonist withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, dysphoria, pain) or a neuroleptic malignant-like picture.
Not asking about impulse control disorders, falls, swallowing and mood at reviews.

drugs.name: Co-careldopa (levodopa with carbidopa)
drugs.dose: 25/100 mg: 1 tablet orally three times daily to start; titrate one tablet at a time to response (SmPC maximum 8 tablets of 25/100 mg daily)
drugs.notes: Nausea, postural hypotension, hallucinations; later wearing off and dyskinesia. Co-beneldopa (levodopa with benserazide) is an alternative, with a dispersible form for nasogastric use.

drugs.name: Pramipexole
drugs.dose: 0.088 mg base (0.125 mg salt) three times daily in week 1, 0.18 mg base three times daily in week 2, 0.35 mg base three times daily in week 3; then increase by 0.54 mg base daily each week if needed; max 3.3 mg base (4.5 mg salt) daily
drugs.notes: Doses are stated as base in the UK and as salt elsewhere. Reduce in renal impairment. Taper when stopping. Sleep attacks, impulse control disorders, oedema.

drugs.name: Ropinirole
drugs.dose: 0.25 mg three times daily for 1 week, then increase by 0.25 mg three times daily each week to 1 mg three times daily; then by 0.5 to 1 mg three times daily weekly; usual 3 to 9 mg daily, max 24 mg daily
drugs.notes: Take with food. Sleepiness, impulse control disorders, hallucinations. Re-titrate if stopped for a day or more.

drugs.name: Rotigotine (transdermal patch)
drugs.dose: Early disease: 2 mg/24 h, increase by 2 mg/24 h weekly to max 8 mg/24 h. Advanced disease: 4 mg/24 h, increase by 2 mg/24 h weekly to max 16 mg/24 h
drugs.notes: Useful when nil by mouth; dose from a levodopa conversion calculator. Site reactions, confusion at high doses.

drugs.name: Rasagiline
drugs.notes: Avoid in moderate and do not use in severe hepatic impairment. Serotonin toxicity risk with pethidine, tramadol and some antidepressants.
